name: The Knowledge Argument
statement: A scientist who knew every physical fact about color still learns something new when she first sees red.
statementAccent: still learns something new when she first sees red
meaning: The knowledge argument is an argument against physicalism in the philosophy of mind, most famously presented by the philosopher Frank Jackson in his 1982 paper Epiphenomenal Qualia and elaborated in his 1986 paper What Mary Didn't Know. It is built around a thought experiment usually called Mary's Room. Mary is a brilliant scientist who has lived her entire life in a black-and-white room and has learned about the world only through black-and-white materials, such as a monochrome television. She comes to know all the physical facts about color vision, everything that physics and neuroscience can tell us about wavelengths, the brain, and the processing of color. Then one day she leaves the room, or is shown a red object, and sees color for the first time. The argument asks whether she learns something new. The intuition Jackson pressed is that she does: she learns what it is like to see red, the felt quality of the experience. But if she already knew all the physical facts, this new knowledge must be knowledge of a fact that is not physical. Therefore, Jackson argued, physicalism is false, because there are facts about conscious experience that are not physical facts. The knowledge argument is one of the most discussed arguments in philosophy of mind, though Jackson himself later abandoned it and became a physicalist.
mechanism: The knowledge argument works by setting up a case in which someone has complete physical knowledge and then seems to gain further knowledge, so that the further knowledge cannot be physical. The steps are these. First, before her release, Mary has complete physical knowledge about color vision: by stipulation she knows every physical fact there is to know about what happens when people see colors, the physics of light, the physiology of the eye, and the neuroscience of color processing. Second, when she leaves the room and sees a colored object for the first time, she seems to learn something new, namely what it is like to see red, the phenomenal character or quale of the color experience. Third, if she already knew all the physical facts yet still learns something on seeing color, then what she learns must be a fact that is not among the physical facts, a non-physical fact about experience. The conclusion is that physicalism, the thesis that all facts are physical facts, is false, since there are facts about conscious experience, facts about qualia, that are not physical. The force of the argument rests on the intuition that Mary genuinely learns something new, and the debate over it largely concerns whether this intuition is correct and, if so, how it should be interpreted, whether as gaining a new fact or something else.

examples.text: Mary, in a black-and-white room, learns every physical fact about color vision without ever seeing color.
When Mary leaves the room and sees a red object, she seems to learn what it is like to see red, something new.
If she knew all the physical facts yet learns something, that fact must be non-physical, so physicalism is false.

variants.name: The ability hypothesis
variants.text: Lewis and Nemirow's reply that Mary gains new abilities, like recognizing and imagining red, not new propositional knowledge.

variants.name: The phenomenal concepts strategy
variants.text: The reply that Mary learns an old physical fact in a new way, acquiring a new concept rather than a new fact.

whyItMatters: The knowledge argument is one of the most influential and widely discussed arguments in the philosophy of mind, offering a vivid and intuitive challenge to physicalism, the dominant view that everything is physical. Through the memorable thought experiment of Mary the color scientist, it distills the worry that no amount of physical knowledge can capture what it is like to have a conscious experience, and it makes the case that there are facts about experience, facts about qualia, that lie beyond the reach of physical science. This places the argument at the center of the debate over consciousness, closely allied with the hard problem of consciousness and the explanatory gap, and it has generated an enormous literature of responses that have sharpened positions on both sides. Physicalist replies, including the ability hypothesis and the phenomenal concepts strategy, have deepened the understanding of what phenomenal knowledge is, and the argument's fate has become a touchstone for the plausibility of physicalism. In a striking twist, Frank Jackson, who devised the argument, later rejected it and became a physicalist, which itself became part of the debate. As the argument that a complete physical knower could still learn what red is like, the knowledge argument is a landmark in the study of consciousness.

working.text: stipulate that Mary knows every physical fact about color vision from within a black-and-white room.
have her leave the room and see red for the first time, apparently learning what it is like.
infer that since she knew all physical facts yet learns something, that fact is non-physical, so physicalism is false.

limits: The knowledge argument is influential but its conclusion is far from accepted, and it faces powerful replies. The ability hypothesis, associated with David Lewis and Laurence Nemirow, holds that Mary gains only new abilities, the know-how to recognize, imagine, and remember color experiences, rather than new propositional knowledge of a fact, so no non-physical fact is learned. The phenomenal concepts strategy, the leading physicalist reply, grants that Mary gains new knowledge but denies she learns a new fact, holding that she acquires new phenomenal concepts that let her represent an already-known physical fact in a new way, so it is an old fact grasped in a new mode of presentation. Strikingly, Frank Jackson himself later abandoned the argument and became a physicalist, adopting a representationalist view. So the knowledge argument robustly presses the intuition that physical knowledge omits what experience is like, understood as a much-contested argument whose anti-physicalist conclusion is resisted by strong replies and was even rejected by its own author.
misreadings: The knowledge argument does not conclusively refute physicalism; its anti-physicalist conclusion is contested, and its own author, Frank Jackson, later abandoned it and became a physicalist. Physicalist replies deny that Mary learns a new fact, holding either that she gains new abilities or that she grasps an old physical fact in a new way. And the argument turns on an intuition that she learns something, which is disputed, so treating the knowledge argument as decisively disproving physicalism, as showing a new fact beyond doubt, or as unanswered, misreads a much-contested argument.
origin: An argument against physicalism presented by Frank Jackson in his 1982 paper Epiphenomenal Qualia, using the Mary's Room thought experiment to argue that a complete physical knower could still learn what an experience is like; later abandoned by Jackson.
